query: How should swab collection and elution be standardized across sites to convert CFU/mL to CFU/swab, and what study design will quantify operator and matrix variability?

response.query: How should swab collection and elution be standardized across sites to convert CFU/mL to CFU/swab, and what study design will quantify operator and matrix variability?
response.answer: Standardize swab collection and elution using CLSI M40-A2 guidelines; quantify variability with a multi-site study comparing CFU/mL to CFU/swab. Use statistical analysis to measure operator and matrix effects.

results.title: Accordance With Approved Standard CLSI M40 -A2.
results.content: Published Time: Thu, 01 Aug 2024 09:26:19 GMT An Evaluation of Faecal Transport Swabs Using the Swab Elution Method in # Accordance With Approved Standard CLSI M40 -A2. The aim of this study was to evaluate and compare the recovery efficacy of three faecal transport swabs using the quantitativ e e lution method of CLSI M40 -A2 adapted for enteric bacteria. The performance of three medical devices were MWE Fecal Transwab ®, a polyurethane foam tip with 2 mL vial of Cary -Blair medium; MWE Fecal Transwab Purflock , a multifilament polyester flocked fibre tip with 2 mL Cary -Blair medium; and Copan FecalSwab ™ , a Nylon® flocked swab with 2 mL of Cary -Blair medium. • For each swab tested, 3 time points (0, 24, 48 & 72h) and two temperatures (RT & 4°C) were used as holding conditions. • For each swab to be tested , and each organism/holding temperature/holding time, 50μl aliquots of the suspension was dispensed into wells of a microtitre plate and used to inoculate the swab. Dilutions were then spiral plated (100μl) on tryptone soya agar using an Neutec ™ Eddy Jet™ • For each swab/organism/temperature, at each holding time, the sampling procedure outlined Plate counts were used to calculate CFU/ml of recovered bacteria. ## DISCUSSION/CONCLUSION The number of viable organisms remained stable when stored at 4 °C and there was less than 1 log change over the 72 hour period for all test organisms and swab types. At RT, the MWE Fecal Transwab ® also maintained viable counts of all three organisms with less than 1 log change in CFU/ml. For the MWE Fecal Transwab PF, at RT, there was a >2 log increase in CFU/ml increase for E. At the same storage condition i.e. RT, there was an increase in viable count for all three organisms with the Copan FecalSwab ™ with 3.02 log CFU/ml increase in recovery for E. At 4°C, the recovery of microorganisms was maintained for 72 h for all three swabs, compared to swabs stored at RT, thus all three swabs were compliant with the M40 -A2 protocol at the cold temperature.

results.title: Evaluation of Liquid-Based Swab Transport Systems against the New Approved CLSI M40-A2 Standard
results.content: #### Roles Received 2015 Dec 22; Revision requested 2015 Dec 31; Accepted 2016 Jan 25; Prepublished 2016 Feb 3; Issue date 2016 Apr. PMC Copyright notice Following revised information pertaining to newer swab types and testing protocols in the new CLSI M40-A2 standard, we evaluated three liquid swab transport systems for the recovery of aerobic, anaerobic, and fastidious organisms at room temperature and at 4°C. All tested liquid swab transport systems were fully compliant with the M40-A2 standard, with acceptable performance at both temperatures after the full specified holding period, using both qualitative (roll-plate) and quantitative (swab elution) methods. The M40-A2 standard indicates that, for bacterial recovery from STSs using the roll-plate method, there should be ≥5 CFU after the specified holding period for specimens held at 4°C or RT, from the same dilution as used in time zero plate counts, in order for the viability assessment to be considered acceptable. Bacterial recovery and overgrowth for foam and flocked swabs over 48 h at room temperature and 4°C, using the roll-plate (qualitative) method Open in a new tab The M40-A2 compliance criteria were yields of ≥5 CFU (or 1-log-unit increase for _P. For the swab elution method, the M40-A2 standard indicates that, for compliance regarding viability, any specimen held at 4°C or RT should yield no more than a 3-log-unit decrease in CFU between time zero and the end of the specified holding period and, for assessment of overgrowth, any specimen held at 4°C should yield no more than a 1-log-unit increase in CFU between time zero and the end of the specified holding period. Prior to the recently published M40-A2 standard, swab transport systems, including the swab tip formats used in this study, were evaluated for viability and recovery using only one test method, i.e., the swab elution method or the roll-plate method (2, 6). In addition, we recommend that commercially available liquid medium transport systems used in conjunction with foam or flocked swabs be internally evaluated using both qualitative and quantitative methods, to ensure the sensitivity of the system, the reliability of the results in clinical settings, and compliance with the M40-A2 standard.

results.title: Distribution and characteristics of bacteria on the hand during oropharyngeal swab collection: Which handwashing points are affected? - Chen - 2024 - Journal of Clinical Nursing - Wiley Online Library
results.content: Among the five sites of the sampling hand, the palm side of the finger was the most contaminated site with a total bacterial count of 3271.7 Cfu/cm2 (IQR = 0.300; 0.000–3.175). The site with the lowest OHR was the dorsal side of the finger and the dorsum of the hand, but the site with the highest number of bacterial contaminations was the palm side of the finger, indicating that the palm side of the finger had individual samples that were severely contaminated. Among the five sites of the auxiliary hand, the interdigital space was the most contaminated site with a total bacterial count of 3147.0 Cfu/cm2 (IQR = 0.000; 0.000–2.250). The median distribution showed that the individual hand sites bacterial counts were higher in the sampling hand than in the auxiliary hand, indicating that the hand holding the oropharyngeal swab were more susceptible to contamination than the hand touching the surrounding objects (Figure S4). This study is the first to quantify bacterial colony counts and areas of the hand at risk of contamination during oropharyngeal swab collection for HCWs. We observed that the most contaminated areas of the sampling hand and the auxiliary hand were the dorsal side of the finger and the dorsum of the hand. Confirmed by the high total bacterial counts detected on both the sampling and auxiliary hands, it appears that there were some exceedingly high levels of bacterial contamination on the hands during oropharyngeal swabbing. Our results show that although the probability of extensive hand contamination after oropharyngeal swab collection is low, but if the patient coughs or sneezes, HCWs should take care to prevent hand contamination through thorough hand hygiene. One study documented that HCWs had an average of 0%–10% contamination of the dorsal side of the finger and the dorsum of the hand and an average of 0%–25% contamination of the palm side of the finger and the Palm after removing contaminated gloves (Alhmidi et al., 2019). The HCW holds the test tube against the ditch of their finger during oropharyngeal swab collection; the test tube is in an exposed environment and may be contaminated, leading to a high number of total bacteria in the interdigital space of the auxiliary hand.
